# Karnak: the stories first, then the spelling

The marks in **Karnak** make the most sense standing next to the myths they have to carry. So the myths come first.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**The Most Select of Places.** The temple theology held that Amun’s staff, planted in the ground of Thebes at the world’s beginning, designated Ipet-isut as his estate — ‘the most select of places’.  Each new king’s building programme was framed not as innovation but as the staff’s ancient will, finally fulfilled.

**The River Journey of the Gods.** In the great Opet festival, Amun’s barque sailed the canal from Karnak to Luxor temple and back — the Theban gods’ annual renewal of their own marriage with the city.  The avenue of ram-headed sphinxes, restored today, was the procession’s road; the festival’s reliefs cover Karnak’s walls.

**The Pharaohs’ Roll Call.** Seti I’s gallery of kings, the Karnak King List, names the legitimate succession from the ancestors — a theology of history in stone, in which every true king is one who kept the ‘Most Select of Places’ in repair.  The list omits the heretics, editing eternity.

## The Name Travels

Karnak housed them all: Amun-Ra supreme, but also Montu, Mut, Khonsu, Ptah and Opet, in a polyphony of chapels that makes the complex a pantheon in plan.  The Greeks called the whole Thebes ‘Diospolis’, city of Zeus-Amun; the temple was the Zeus-estate, and Alexander the Great crossed the desert to its oracle to be confirmed son of Amun.
